```{r setup}
library(bssd)
```

```{r helpers, include = FALSE}
# results and settings of the installed reproduction and validation scripts
read_results <- function(folder, name) {
  read.csv(system.file(folder, "results", name, package = "bssd",
                       mustWork = TRUE), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
# value assigned at the top level of an installed validation script
script_value <- function(script, name) {
  exprs <- parse(system.file("validation", script, package = "bssd",
                             mustWork = TRUE))
  for (e in exprs) {
    if (is.call(e) && identical(e[[1L]], as.name("<-")) &&
        identical(e[[2L]], as.name(name))) {
      return(eval(e[[3L]], baseenv()))
    }
  }
  stop("'", name, "' is not assigned in ", script, call. = FALSE)
}
fmt <- function(x, digits = 4) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
fmt_e <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "e", digits = 1)
fmt_n <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "d", big.mark = ",")
# MCMC comparisons of a validation script. The tolerance of each item is four
# Monte Carlo standard errors. For the median, the reference is 0.5 and the
# compared value is the MCMC proportion of draws below the bssd median.
mcmc_table <- function(v, rr = "r") {
  v <- v[v$judgement != "INFO", ]
  stat <- sub("^.*_", "", v$id)
  med <- stat == "MED"
  quantity <- stat
  is_p <- grepl("^P[0-9]", stat)
  quantity[is_p] <- sprintf("P(%s > %s)", rr, sub("^P", "", stat[is_p]))
  quantity[stat == "PROB"] <- sub(" [|] data[)].*$", ")",
                                  v$quantity[stat == "PROB"])
  quantity[med] <- sprintf("P(%s <= bssd median)", rr)
  quantity[stat == "MEAN"] <- sprintf("mean of %s", rr)
  quantity[stat == "IPP"] <- "placebo incidence"
  quantity[stat == "IPD"] <- "study drug incidence"
  bssd_value <- ifelse(med, v$reference, v$bssd)
  mcmc_value <- ifelse(med, v$bssd, v$reference)
  data.frame(data = sub("^[A-Z]+_([A-Z][0-9]+)_.*$", "\\1", v$id),
             quantity = quantity, bssd = bssd_value, mcmc = mcmc_value,
             difference = bssd_value - mcmc_value, se = v$tolerance / 4,
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
show_mcmc <- function(m) {
  knitr::kable(data.frame(Data = m$data, Quantity = m$quantity,
                          bssd = fmt(m$bssd), MCMC = fmt(m$mcmc),
                          Difference = fmt_e(m$difference),
                          SE = fmt_e(m$se),
                          Ratio = fmt(abs(m$difference) / m$se, 2)),
               align = "llrrrrr")
}
# effective sample sizes of the posterior probabilities P(r > c)
ess_range <- function(v) {
  note <- v$note[grepl("_(PROB|P[0-9.]+)$", v$id)]
  range(as.numeric(sub("^.*ESS ([0-9]+).*$", "\\1", note)))
}
# comparison of the default integration grid with a finer grid or with the
# Python reference (validate_convergence.R)
show_convergence <- function(v) {
  parts <- regmatches(v$quantity, regexec(paste0(
    "^(.*), (finer grid vs default|Python reference vs default|",
    "Python reference vs finer grid), (.*)$"), v$quantity))
  parts <- do.call(rbind, parts)
  err <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(sub("^reported error ", "", v$note)))
  knitr::kable(data.frame(Data = parts[, 4], Comparison = parts[, 3],
                          Quantity = sub(" [|] data[)]$", ")", parts[, 2]),
                          Reference = fmt(v$reference, 6),
                          bssd = fmt(v$bssd, 6),
                          Difference = fmt_e(v$abs_diff),
                          `Error estimate` = ifelse(is.na(err), "",
                                                    fmt_e(err)),
                          check.names = FALSE),
               align = "lllrrrr")
}
```

## Model

BDRIBS (Bayesian Detection of potential Risk using Inference on Blinded
Safety data) is the model of Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018). Duncan (2026,
Section 3.2.2) calls it BDRIBS(1) when the exposure is the total exposure
time of the blinded population. The number of subjects with the event in the
blinded data, $Y$, follows
$$Y \sim \mathrm{Poisson}\{E \delta (r k + 1) / (k + 1)\},$$
where $E$ is the total exposure time, $\delta$ is the event rate on placebo,
$r$ is the rate ratio of the study drug to placebo, and the study drug and
placebo are randomized in the ratio $k:1$. The priors are
$$\delta \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\lambda_{HP} PT_{HP} / DF, PT_{HP} / DF), \quad r = \frac{p}{k (1 - p)}, \quad p \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a, b),$$
where the Gamma distribution has the shape and rate parameters,
$\lambda_{HP}$ and $PT_{HP}$ are the event rate and the total patient time of
historical placebo data, and $DF$ is a discount factor for the historical
data. The parameter $p$ is the probability that an event in the blinded data
occurred on the study drug. A signal is declared when
$P(r > \theta_c \mid Y) > P_{\mathrm{cutoff}}$.

The arguments of `bdribs_post()` correspond to the symbols as follows.

| Symbol | Argument | Description |
|---|---|---|
| $Y$ | `y` | number of subjects with the event |
| $E$ | `exposure` | total exposure time, the sum of the follow-up times |
| $k$ | `k` | randomization ratio of study drug to placebo |
| $\lambda_{HP}$ | `lambda_hp` | event rate in the historical placebo data |
| $PT_{HP}$ | `pt_hp` | total patient time of the historical placebo data; `Inf` fixes $\delta$ at `lambda_hp` |
| $DF$ | `df` | discount factor |
| $(a, b)$ | `p_prior` | shape parameters of the Beta prior of $p$ (default `r deparse(formals(bdribs_post)$p_prior)`) |
| $\theta_c$ | `rr0` | critical value of $r$ (default `r formals(bdribs_post)$rr0`) |
| $P_{\mathrm{cutoff}}$ | `cutoff` | posterior probability threshold (default `r formals(bdribs_post)$cutoff`) |

The exposure, `lambda_hp`, `pt_hp` and the optional time `t_star` for the
cumulative incidences must be in the same time unit.

## Example: hypothetical example 2 of Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018)

In Section 4.4 of Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018), the study drug and placebo are
randomized 2:1, the blinded data have 540 patient-years of exposure, and the
background rate on placebo is about 0.011 per patient-year, estimated from 33
events in about 3000 patient-years of historical data.

### Screening analysis

The screening analysis treats the background rate as known
(`pt_hp = Inf`) and uses the uniform prior for $p$. Mukhopadhyay et al.
(2018, Sections 3.4 and 4.4) compare the posterior probability with the
boundary $3 / (3 + k \theta_c)$, which is used here as `cutoff`.

```{r screening}
screen <- expand.grid(rr0 = c(1, 1.3), y = c(8, 9))
screen$cutoff <- 3 / (3 + 2 * screen$rr0)
screen$prob <- mapply(function(y, rr0, cutoff) {
  bdribs_post(y = y, exposure = 540, k = 2, lambda_hp = 0.011, pt_hp = Inf,
              p_prior = c(1, 1), rr0 = rr0, cutoff = cutoff,
              details = FALSE)$prob
}, screen$y, screen$rr0, screen$cutoff)
screen$signal <- screen$prob > screen$cutoff
```

```{r screening-table, echo = FALSE}
mukh <- read_results("reproduce", "reproduce_Mukhopadhyay2018.csv")
published <- function(id) mukh$published[match(id, mukh$id)]
screen$published <- published(c("M_EX2_1", "M_EX2_2", "M_EX2_3", "M_EX2_4"))
knitr::kable(screen[, c("y", "rr0", "cutoff", "prob", "signal", "published")],
             digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Events", "rr0", "Boundary", "bssd", "Signal",
                           "Mukhopadhyay et al."))
```

The published values were computed by MCMC with the bdribs package, and they
differ from the values of bssd by at most
`r fmt(max(abs(screen$prob - screen$published)), 3)`. With 9 events, the
posterior is

```{r screening-print}
fit9 <- bdribs_post(y = 9, exposure = 540, k = 2, lambda_hp = 0.011,
                    pt_hp = Inf, p_prior = c(1, 1))
fit9
```

### Sensitivity analysis

In the second step, the screening analysis is repeated with background rates
at the limits of the 90% credible interval of the background rate. As in
Section 4.3 of the article, the interval is computed from the Gamma
distribution with the number of historical events plus 0.5 as the shape and
the historical patient-years plus 0.5 as the rate.

```{r sensitivity}
rate_ci <- qgamma(c(0.05, 0.95), shape = 33 + 0.5, rate = 3000 + 0.5)
rate_ci
sens <- expand.grid(rr0 = c(1, 1.3), lambda_hp = rate_ci)
sens$prob <- mapply(function(lambda_hp, rr0) {
  bdribs_post(y = 9, exposure = 540, k = 2, lambda_hp = lambda_hp,
              pt_hp = Inf, p_prior = c(1, 1), rr0 = rr0,
              details = FALSE)$prob
}, sens$lambda_hp, sens$rr0)
```

```{r sensitivity-table, echo = FALSE}
sens$published <- published(c("M_EX2_13", "M_EX2_15", "M_EX2_12",
                              "M_EX2_14"))
knitr::kable(sens[, c("lambda_hp", "rr0", "prob", "published")],
             digits = c(4, 1, 3, 2), row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Background rate", "rr0", "bssd",
                           "Mukhopadhyay et al."))
```

The interval (`r fmt(rate_ci[1])`, `r fmt(rate_ci[2])`) agrees with the
interval (`r published("M_EX2_10")`, `r published("M_EX2_11")`) of Section 4.4
of the article. The posterior probabilities differ from the published values,
which are given to two decimal places, by at most
`r fmt(max(abs(sens$prob - sens$published)), 3)`.

Instead of fixing the background rate, the historical data can be used as
the Gamma prior of $\delta$, which gives the posterior probability
unconditional on the background rate (Mukhopadhyay et al., 2018,
Section 4.3):

```{r gamma-prior}
fit_gamma <- bdribs_post(y = 9, exposure = 540, k = 2,
                         lambda_hp = (33 + 0.5) / (3000 + 0.5),
                         pt_hp = 3000 + 0.5, df = 1, p_prior = c(1, 1))
fit_gamma
```

### Total exposure time from subject-level data

For subject-level data, `time_at_risk()` returns the total exposure time
(`exposure`), which BDRIBS(1) uses, and the total time at risk, which
BDRIBS(2) uses (`vignette("bdribs2")`).

```{r exposure}
time_at_risk(follow_up = c(52, 52, 30, 12), event = c(1, 0, 1, 0),
             event_time = c(10, NA, 25, NA))
```

## Numerical integration

Because the Gamma prior of $\delta$ is conjugate to the Poisson likelihood,
`bdribs_post()` integrates $\delta$ out analytically. The remaining posterior
quantities are one-dimensional integrals over $\mathrm{logit}(p)$, which are
computed by adaptive quadrature (`stats::integrate()`) with a relative
tolerance of $10^{-10}$ (see `?bdribs_post`). The expected values of the
tests in `tests/testthat` were computed beforehand by independent Python
implementations (`inst/validation/python/ref_bdribs.py` and
`ref_bdribs_fixed.py`).

## Comparison with MCMC

```{r mcmc-data, include = FALSE}
v <- read_results("validation", "validate_bdribs_package.csv")
m <- mcmc_table(v)
cases <- script_value("validate_bdribs_package.R", "cases")
n_iter <- script_value("validate_bdribs_package.R", "n_iter")
n_chain <- script_value("validate_bdribs_package.R", "n_chain")
src <- readLines(system.file("validation", "validate_bdribs_package.R",
                             package = "bssd", mustWork = TRUE))
n_burn <- as.numeric(sub("^.*burn = ([0-9]+).*$", "\\1",
                         grep("burn = [0-9]+", src, value = TRUE)[1L]))
ess <- ess_range(v)
is_prob <- grepl("^P[(]", m$quantity)
```

The bdribs package of Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018) samples the same model by
MCMC with JAGS. The script `inst/validation/validate_bdribs_package.R`
compares `bdribs_post()` with `bdribs::bdribs()` for the settings below. The
results in this section are read from the output of that script
(`validate_bdribs_package.csv` in the folder `validation/results` of the
installed package); JAGS is not run when this article is built.

```{r mcmc-settings, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Data = cases$id, y = cases$y, E = cases$pyr, k = cases$k,
  `Historical events` = cases$bg_events,
  `Historical patient-years` = cases$bg_pyr,
  `Background rate` = ifelse(cases$inf_type == 1, "fixed (inf.type = 1)",
                             "Gamma prior (inf.type = 2)"),
  `Prior of p` = sprintf("Beta(%g, %g)", cases$a, cases$b),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE)
```

With `inf.type = 1`, `bdribs::bdribs()` fixes the background rate at the
historical events divided by the historical patient-years, which is
`bdribs_post()` with `pt_hp = Inf`. With `inf.type = 2`, it uses the Gamma
prior with the shape (historical events + 0.001) and the rate (historical
patient-years + 0.001), which is `bdribs_post()` with these values as
`lambda_hp * pt_hp` and `pt_hp` and `df = 1`. `bdribs::bdribs()` was run with
`r n_chain` chains, `r fmt_n(n_burn)` burn-in iterations and
`r fmt_n(n_iter)` iterations (the arguments `nc`, `burn` and `iter` of
`mc.params`). The Monte Carlo standard error (SE) of each MCMC estimate uses
the effective sample size of the draws (`coda::effectiveSize()`); for the
posterior probabilities, the effective sample sizes are between
`r fmt_n(ess[1])` and `r fmt_n(ess[2])`. For the median, the table shows the
MCMC
proportion of draws below the posterior median computed by bssd, which should
be 0.5. The column Ratio is the absolute difference divided by the SE.

```{r mcmc-table, echo = FALSE}
show_mcmc(m)
```

In all `r nrow(m)` items, the bssd value is within
`r fmt(max(abs(m$difference) / m$se), 1)` standard errors of the MCMC value,
and `r sum(abs(m$difference) / m$se <= 2)` items are within two standard
errors. The largest absolute difference in a posterior probability is
`r fmt(max(abs(m$difference[is_prob])))`, while the SEs of the MCMC
probabilities are between `r fmt(min(m$se[is_prob]))` and
`r fmt(max(m$se[is_prob]))`. Differences of this size are expected from the
Monte Carlo error of MCMC alone, so the difference between the numerical
integration of bssd and MCMC is negligible in practice. The validation script
judges an item PASS when the difference is at most four standard errors;
`r sum(v$judgement == "PASS")` of the `r nrow(v)` items are PASS.
